On a straight road, car A starts with an acceleration of $2\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, while car B passes by car A at a constant speed of $10\mathrm{m/s}$.

1. Before car A catches up with car B, when is the distance between the two cars the greatest? When does car A catch up with car B?
2. When vehicle A accelerates to $24\mathrm{m/s}$, it immediately stops accelerating and begins to brake with an acceleration of $6\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$. Find the time when vehicles A and B meet for the second time (referring to the time from when vehicle A starts until it meets vehicle B for the second time).

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Take t = 0 as the instant when car B passes car A, and take their common position then as x = 0. Car A starts from rest with acceleration 2 m/s^2, so x_A = (1/2)(2)t^2 = t^2. Car B moves at constant speed 10 m/s, so x_B = 10t. Before A catches B, the separation is d(t) = x_B - x_A = 10t - t^2. This quadratic has its maximum at t = -b/(2a) = -10/(2(-1)) = 5 s. For catch-up, set x_A = x_B: t^2 = 10t, so t = 0 or t = 10 s. The nonzero catch-up time is 10 s. For the changed motion in part 2, A accelerates until its speed reaches 24 m/s. Since v = at = 2t, this takes t = 12 s. Its displacement then is x_A = (1/2)(2)(12^2) = 144 m. After that A brakes with acceleration magnitude 6 m/s^2. The braking time until stop is 24/6 = 4 s, so A stops at t = 16 s. The additional braking distance is v^2/(2a) = 24^2/(2*6) = 48 m, so A's stopping position is x_A = 144 + 48 = 192 m. Car B continues at x_B = 10t. When B reaches A's stopped position, 10t = 192, so t = 19.2 s. This is the second meeting time measured from when A starts.
